# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
  (see-test-fail)
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
  (mechanism-meant-survive)
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
  (simulator-stateful-mechanism)
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
  (trusting-new-transform)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
  (test-stubs-exact)
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
  (test-dereferences-path)
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
  (test-value-set)
- **Naming the thing a fixture stands for** - invent the name (`acme-pack`, `acme-user`,
  `acme.example`) wherever the case holds for any name at all, and keep a real one only where that
  entity is what the case asserts about: a borrowed name reads as meaningful, collides with the
  real thing's own cases, and makes every later rename an edit of tests that were never about it.
  (fixture-names-invented)
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite. (testing-tasks-precondition)
- **Asserting on a record the code under test produced** — a finding, a parsed spec, a normalized declaration — assert the fields that code **computed**, and leave the ones it copied straight through from its own declaration or from your setup. A check selected by its id whose test then reads `finding.rule` back, or restates the `on_fail` its declaration set, is asserting the selector: it stays green however wrong the matching is, and goes red only when someone deliberately renames or re-grades the rule. One computed field identifies a record — the rest is your setup talking back to you.
  (asserting-record-code)
- **A coupling that must hold for every member of a set** — each task's id matching the directory it is discovered by, each check's `doc:` pointer resolving, each declaration validating — assert it once in a sweep that reads the whole set out of the tree, never in each member's own suite. The per-member copy only ever holds the members that happen to have a suite, so it under-covers and taxes at the same time: the shape is billed to each suite that has one while the members without one go unguarded.
  (coupling-must-hold)
- **Pinning the text a finding or error carries** — assert the part the code **derived** from the input (the version it tells you to bump to, the path it resolved, the term it names), and leave the static sentence alone. A remedy's wording is prose someone will improve, and asserted back it turns every rewording into a test edit while guarding nothing — those words were read straight out of the declaration the test already points at.
  (pinning-text-finding)
- **Sweeping a set** — a tree walk, a filter over a file's lines, a loop over discovered
  members — **pin how many members it covered**, beside the loop. An assertion reached only
  inside a loop, or only behind an `if`, says nothing about the members that never entered it,
  so a set that quietly shrinks — a renamed token, a moved directory, one call kind of two
  dropping out — leaves the survivors passing and reports that pass for the whole. A count read
  off the same source is the pin (`assert.ok(files.length >= 25)`), and a guard *inside* the
  loop needs its own, since the
  outer count says nothing about how many members reached the assertion behind it. (sweeping-set)
- **Reading the source *text* of a module the test could `import`** — asserting an identifier
  appears in it, or that one string precedes another in the file — inverts the signal: it goes
  red on a pure rename and stays green on a behaviour change that leaves the tokens in place.
  Grepping a *different* artifact is the two-artifact drift guard above and stays. Where the
  module is callable and a grep is still the only way in, report that its entry point does the
  whole job at once — that is worth more than the assertion. (reading-source-text)
- **Choosing the cases for a validator, parser or guard** — its own rejection branches are the
  list: for each, write the input that forces it. A branch nothing forces is either a promise
  no test holds or one the code can no longer reach, and both are worth finding. The gap
  clusters on the **present-but-unusable** input — the empty string, the directory that will
  not read, the module that throws on import — because absent and valid are the two cases
  everyone writes, while the field that is there and broken is the one that arrives in
  production. (choosing-cases-validator)
- **A comparison against a threshold, a deadline or an anchor instant** — test the value
  exactly **on** it, not only either side. `<=` and `<` differ on exactly one input, so a suite
  that samples comfortably around the boundary agrees with both and pins neither. Where a cron
  or a poll drives the comparison, that one input is the ordinary case rather than the edge: the
  run fires *at* the anchor. (comparison-against-threshold)
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
  (prefer-single-shared)
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
  (wire-format-encoding)
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism.
  (traceability-coverage-gate)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
  (golden-snapshot-test)
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
  (snapshot-golden-test-2)
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
  (round-trip-test)
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
  (new-e2e-heavy)
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
  (test-can-only)
- **A shared fixture helper is paid for by every test that calls it**, so build the part that is identical for every case — a scratch repo's `init` and seed commit, a migrated database, a compiled bundle — once per process and copy it, rather than rebuilding it per test.
  (shared-fixture-helper)

- **A test runner parallelises across FILES, so one file's serial runtime is a floor no worker count clears.** When a suite's CPU sits well below its core count, the idle cores are waiting on that file — give it intra-file concurrency, which more workers cannot substitute for.
  (test-runner-parallelises)

- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
  (run-suite-know)
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically.
  (test-code-drives)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
  (gate-fuzzy-quality)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
  (behavior-person-must)
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
  (snapshot-golden-test)
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
  (test-asserts-exact)
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
  (test-maintains-committed)
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
  (render-ui-image)
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
  (reproduce-reported-golden)
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).
  (image-golden-surface)

1: # packs/ — the corpus content, active by declaration
2: 
3: Each `packs/<name>/` bundles a pack's **prose** (`RULES.md`, injected at session start when the pack is active), its **checks** (run at every Stop), and its **bundled skills** (`<pack>/skills/`, mounted at session start). **No pack is active by default** — every pack, the `basics` baseline included, activates only when declared in `.claudinite-settings.json` (bootstrap's `--init` seeds `basics` plus the fingerprinted technology packs; the nightly update backfills the explicit `basics` declaration into existing consumers). Discovery is structural — any `packs/<name>/pack.mjs` is a pack, and that manifest is the pack's index: what it owns, the checks it runs in each scope, the skills it bundles. A pack's `README.md` is **optional** and carries only what the manifest cannot — provenance, design rationale, an index of its prose. == engine/migrations/README.md 1
1: # Baseline migrations (`engine/migrations/`) — declared path relocations, applied by each member itself
2: 
3: > The **baseline migrations** mechanism, and the machinery that runs it (this README,
4: > `registry.mjs`, `apply.mjs`). Every migration ever landed lives in one folder —
5: > `<landed-date>-<slug>/migration.mjs` — **under the flow that owns it**: an engine change beside
6: > this file, a pack's own change under `packs/<pack>/migrations/`
7: > (docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md §3.7). Discovery walks both, so a caller never asks which.
8: > Records are never retired, archived, or deleted: the full history is the durable backfill
9: > source, and **fetching decides relevance** — vendoring ships a consumer only the records landed
10: > within the last 7 days, while a dormant project baselining out of a fresh canon clone sees them
11: > all and applies what it needs. The code identifiers stay `*Migrations`; "baseline migration" is
12: > what to call the mechanism.
13: 
14: When the canon renames or relocates an artifact that consumers hold their own copy of — a tracked
15: file, a `settings.json` registration, a stub, a path a check or script references — the consumer's
16: copy doesn't move on its own. Historically each such rename grew its own scattered tolerance
17: (`LEGACY_STUB_NAMES` in a check, a `.gitkeep` fallback in the sync script and again in the census, a
18: Part-3b step in bootstrap) with **no single home**. A **baseline migration** closes that gap: one
19: declarative record per rename, discovered structurally (any `<flow>/migrations/<date>-<slug>/migration.mjs`,
20: like packs and skills), that supplies the read-side resolver and the write-side rename.
21: 
22: ## A baseline migration
23: 
24: ```js
25: // An illustrative record (the shape, not a live migration): the historical
== engine/migrations/README.md 86
86: There is no retirement, no archive, and no TTL mover. All records are equal; three readers each take
87: the slice they need:
88: 
89: - **Apply/backfill** ([`loadMigrations`](registry.mjs)) loads **every** record present. In a fresh
90:   canon clone that is the full history, so a dormant project that fell behind and only now baselines
91:   still catches up on everything it missed — `apply.mjs` is idempotent, so records it already
92:   applied are no-ops.

# Searching for a tool

- **A search that finds nothing** is evidence about your query, not about the environment: vary
  the query before concluding a capability is absent, and try the tool before telling the owner a
  step is theirs. (search-finds-nothing)
- **`select:` takes a short name as readily as a qualified one** — `select:get_teams` and
  `select:mcp__github__get_teams` both return the tool, and a comma-separated list loads several at
  once. Qualify a name two servers could both carry. (select-takes-short)
- **A bare short name is a keyword query, and resolves too** — `get_teams` on its own returns the
  tool, ranked above the looser matches beneath it. (bare-short-name)
- **A server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names** is the one exception: one
  miss there is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query. (server-whole-roster)

{"number":2181,"title":"Take the retired taskScheduler anchor keys off the accepted list","body":"Not-before: 2026-10-11

`taskScheduler.dailyHour`, `weeklyDay` and `monthlyDay` are retired: a cadence measures whole UTC periods, and the scheduler workflow's cron hours are derived from the repo name at scaffold. Nothing reads them.

They are still **accepted** by `loadConfig`, because `SCHEDULE_KEYS` is an allow-list and an unknown key is a blocking settings error. Removing them before members have converged would turn every member's checks red over a key nothing reads.

```js
// engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs
// @legacy-tolerance advisory:legacy-shape-in-use retire:#2181
export const RETIRED_SCHEDULE_KEYS = ['dailyHour', 'weeklyDay', 'monthlyDay'];
```

## What clears it

- The `cadence-without-anchors` migration record (`packs/claudinite-tasks/migrations/2026-09-20-cadence-without-anchors/`) strips the keys from each member's own `.claudinite-settings.json` on its next converge.
- `legacy-shape-in-use` fires an advisory in any repo still holding one, so a holder that has not converged knows.

## The window

Gated on a convergence window this change states for itself, not on a census: the canon cannot see which repos are active, inert or long stale, so "no member still declares it" never reads true and the tolerance would stand forever.

The window closes on the date in the block above, three weeks after the record lands, which is two full weekly converge cycles plus slack.

## The change

Delete `RETIRED_SCHEDULE_KEYS` and its three entries in `SCHEDULE_KEYS`, and the branch in `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/worldRules/legacy-shape-in-use.mjs` that reads it. A member that ignored the advisory for the window then gets a settings error naming the key, with `remove it` as the fix, which is correct.

Refs #1995

# The LIVE CANARY (#593 phase 3) — the required final step of any core change.
#
# The fixture rehearsal (vendoring/rehearsal/) is the fast gate: hermetic,
# seconds, on every PR. It has one honest weakness — a fixture only tests what
# someone remembered to model. This is the other half: a REAL repo, really
# adopting Claudinite, really running its own scheduler, converged against this
# canon ref and asked whether it still works.
#
# WHY IT IS A SEPARATE WORKFLOW. It takes minutes, needs a cross-repo token, and
# mutates another repository's working tree. A gate with those properties cannot
# run on every push without becoming something people route around. So: manual
# dispatch, plus automatic on merge to main — the post-merge smoke test, which
# the owner's own framing settles as "still much much better than not knowing".
#
# WHERE THE CANARY IS NAMED. In `.claudinite-settings.json`, on the `local/claudinite`
# pack entry's `config.canaryRepo` — the same tracked pack-entry config mechanism
# the claudinite-fleet-sheepdog pack uses for its fleet scope. NOT a GitHub repository variable: the
# binding between this canon and its canary is a fact about the project, and a
# repository variable is invisible in the tree, absent from every diff, and cannot
# be reviewed alongside the workflow that acts on it. A reader of this repo should
# be able to see which repo CI is about to rewrite.
#
# WHY A DEDICATED REPO, NOT A REAL PROJECT. A rehearsal rewrites the mount and
# can leave a failed converge behind. Pointing that at EdFringeNow means a bad
# canon commit leaves a real project dirty at the exact moment attention is
# elsewhere. The canary is disposable by construction; that is its whole value.
#
# WHAT PROTECTS THE CANARY ITSELF: the worker's rehearsal mode
# (CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF) converges, reports, and then RESTORES the working tree —
# no commit, no branch, no PR, and above all no stamp. Stamping a branch head
# would leave the canary `ref-not-on-trunk`, which vendoring's #328 anti-rewind
# guard then refuses to converge over: a rehearsal that wedges its own canary.
name: Canary rehearsal

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Canon ref to rehearse (blank = this workflow's own ref)"
        required: false

input.title: Rename a check's severity to on_fail: block | advise; retire the baseline/converge vocabulary
input.body:
Owner terminology decisions of 2026-09-25 (research: `product-wiki/Terminology/divergences/README.md` in missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite).

## 1. `severity: blocking | advisory` → `on_fail: block | advise`

- Every declared check (121 entries), every coded check, the engine's findings pipeline (`finding`, `applyGrace`, `applyConfig`, the report, the PreToolUse judge) and the settings overrides (`"off" | "advise" | "block"`) use the new spelling.
- **Unchanged, by owner decision:** report text still prints `[BLOCKING]` / `[ADVISORY]` and `N blocking, M advisory`; the pack READMEs' Severity (impact) and Enforcement columns; the usage counters (`blocking` / `advisory`), which the usage fold parses from that report text.
- **Legacy tolerance, one convergence window:** the engine still reads `severity` on a rule, a declaration, a finding and an override value, and mirrors it on every finding so a member's own tests that read `finding.severity` stay green. The markers read `retire:#0` until the removal issue is filed; that's the plan question below.
- **Advisory:** `legacy-shape-in-use` now names an override still spelled `blocking` / `advisory`, and a local pack's declared or coded check that still carries `severity`.
- **Migration record** `engine/migrations/2026-09-25-on-fail-rename`: a named codemod (`renameOnFail`) respells the member's own settings overrides, local declared checks and local check modules in one update pass. It runs only once the member's mount holds the engine that reads `on_fail`, and leaves the member's tests and the vendored mount alone.
- **Delivery:** the engine is released as `60925.1` and every pack's `minEngineVersion` rises to it, because an older engine throws on a declared check with no `severity`. The `engine/RELEASES.md` row is added once the canary rehearsal passes against this branch.
- **Side fix:** `named-import-of-new-engine-export` read an edited export line (a changed signature, an `ENGINE_VERSION` bump) as a brand-new export. The added-lines value source now drops a value that a removed line of the same file also carried.

## 2. Retire the baseline / converge vocabulary

Lands on this branch as its own commits (see below).

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — `packs/*/test/*.test.mjs` reports nothing wrong over 125 of 314 files — while
  `node --test <dir>` fails outright and a glob matching nothing exits 1, so only a glob that
  matches a subset leaves you believing a green run. (whole-suite-command)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (read-runs-output)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which.
  (git-add-new)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (iterating-sweep-across)
- **Editing a `RULES.md` or `README.md` under `packs/`** — the file that holds a pack's rule index
  in step with its prose sits outside the pack, and neither conformance sweep runs it, so add
  `node --test engine-tests/rule-index.test.mjs` to the files the edit touches. (editing-rules-md)

content.content:
## What you write

**One issue, well defined.** The run that implements it will never see this
conversation — the issue body is the whole brief. State the change, the files or
surfaces it touches if you know them, what "done" looks like, and anything the
owner ruled out. Size it to its idea; a rename is a sentence.

**Every field a run reads is one block on the first lines of the description**,
above the marker and ahead of your prose — the waits and the parameters together,
verbatim in this spelling:

```
Blocked-by: #<what this waits on>
Not-before: <ISO instant this may first run>
Model: <opus | sonnet | haiku>
Automerge: <policy>
Task: <pack>/<task>

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

<the brief>
```

Write only the lines the deferral actually has; each is explained below. A field
further down the body still parses, but nobody editing the issue can then see what
the run will do, and a retry that rewrites `Not-before:` has no one place to write
it. (1)

The two waits compose: an issue carrying both sleeps until every blocker has
closed **and** the moment has passed.

**What issue it waits on**, first match wins:

1. the issue of the **previous `/do-later` you filed in this session** — that is
   the chain the owner asked for, each deferral behind the last;
2. otherwise the **pull request** the session's work is on, if one is open;
3. otherwise the **issue** the session is working on;
4. otherwise nothing — omit the field, and say in your reply that it queues
   immediately.

Only ever name blockers that will actually *close* — a merged PR does, a branch
does not. If you filed an earlier `/do-later` this session but no longer have its
number, find it by its marker line among the repo's open issues rather than
falling back to (2).

**What moment it waits on.** A deferral the owner words as a *time* — "check
tomorrow", "in a week", "not until after the release" — waits on an instant, and
`Blocked-by:` cannot express it. That is `Not-before:`, and it is the queue's own
wait field rather than a parameter: it is honoured whether or not the author holds
push access. Give it an ISO-8601 instant resolved against today's date
(`Not-before: 2026-08-28T09:00:00Z`) — the next scheduler run adopts the issue,
holds it blocked, and releases it on the first hourly pass after that instant.
A time-worded deferral is never case 4: it waits on the moment even when no issue
or PR is in flight, so it does not "queue immediately".

## The mark, and the parameters in the body

**The mark is one label**: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`** (`mcp__github__issue_write`,
`labels`). The next scheduler run adopts the issue — writing its machine block
into the body and giving it a status — and the issue itself becomes the work
item, so the whole run plays out where the owner is already looking. Nothing else
is a label any more; everything below rides the issue **body**, and is honoured
only for an author with push access on the repository.

- **`Model: <family>`** — the family **this** session is running, so the deferred
  work is done by what the owner is working with now. Read it with `get_session`

I've finished all five steps on local branch `vocab-update-retirement`, which is not pushed and has no PR. The full suite passes (3926 tests), both sweeps exit 0 with nothing blocking, and nothing I committed changes `severity`/`blocking`/`advisory`.

**Commits** (on `bd944ef`):
1. `54dddf6` Retire "baseline" from the adopt-claudinite trigger text. The description now ends "…or set up Claudinite, or to re-vendor a repo's mount to pick up updates." The skills index was regenerated.
2. `d34d1e5` Rename the sheepdog lever fleet-baseline to fleet-update. This moves the task folder, `force-fleet-update.mjs` (was `force-fleet-baseline.mjs`), the tests and the provenance file. It updates every live reference, including `fleet-token.mjs`, the pack README/RULES and `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md` (forcing-fleet-delivery). The run report's `converged`/`did-not-converge` outcomes are now `updated`/`did-not-update`. It adds the migration record and a test for it (I watched the test fail before it passed). Historical names such as the retired `fleet-baseline.yml` stay as they were.
3. `360bd81` Retire the baseline vocabulary from live prose and comments. "The baseline pack" now reads basics, "baseline migration" reads migration record, and present-tense "baselining" reads the update. The directory and skills index were regenerated.
4. `783561b` Fixes an existing test that my record broke. `pack-update.test.mjs` used a member at integer `99` to mean "past every record", but an integer counts as `99.0`, which is below the new record's `60925.1`.
5. `b51f231` Say "update" where live prose meant the nightly converge (about 150 lines). Work-item uses of "converge" and module names like `converge-wiring.mjs` and `converge-scope.mjs` are unchanged. The "every converge rewrites it" header in both generated index files now says "every update", so every member's index files will be rewritten once on their next update.

**Migration record** (`packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/migrations/2026-09-25-fleet-update-rename/migration.mjs`):
- **Where members hold the old id:** only in `.claudinite-settings.json` → `taskScheduler.disabledTasks`. The record rewrites the quoted id `"claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline"` to the new one. Its `legacyPresent` check reports whether the old id is still in that file.
- **No read-side tolerance, so there's no `@legacy-tolerance` marker and no `retire:#TBD` issue to file.**
  - The lever only runs when someone requests it, so a stale `disabledTasks` entry disables nothing.
  - Open work items under the old id are already closed by the queue's existing handling of undeclared tasks, both when blocked and when picked up.
  - Task history is the queue itself, so a renamed task just reads as never having run.
- **`version: '60925.1'`:** pack versions are cut on `main` after merge, so the record can't know its exact number. I used the next number the bump would cut for the pack at `60922.6`, the same convention as the `task-cadence-terms` and `tidy-repo-absorbed` records, with their "re-check on every rebase" comment. If `main` bumps sheepdog to `60925.1` or higher before this lands, raise it.
- **Why not a far-ahead number** like `claudinite-growth`'s `provenance-marking` (`60930.1`): `versionsInEffect` (`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/install.mjs:230`) lifts a fresh install's stamp to a pending record's version. That stamp would skip pack versions cut before that date. I believe `provenance-marking` has that problem today for fresh installs of claudinite-growth; it's worth checking.

**Things I left on purpose or wasn't sure about:**
- **Environment variables:** the sweep's `FLEET_BASELINE_*` names are unchanged. If someone runs it by hand with the old `DRY_RUN` name after a rename, it would run live instead of dry.
- **Workflow comments:** "converge nightly" is still in the comments of `.github/workflows/claudinite-{scheduler,executor}.yml` and their `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/` copies. Members' copies are never re-copied, so changing the stub could make every member's copy read as stale.
- **Historical text:** design docs (`engine/checks/DESIGN.md`, `vendoring/DESIGN.md`), existing migration records, incident notes (for example `engine/selftest.mjs`'s #518), the `served-by.mjs` value `'baselining'`, the dashboard's commit-message regex, and the acceptance reasons in `.claudinite-settings.json`.
- **Stale rule text I didn't guess at:** the local rule "(`basics/baselining` is the deliberate exception.)" (writing-task-output) names a task that no longer exists. `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/README.md` still describes the guard between baselining and the update flows in the present tense.
- **Ambiguous "converge":** in `converge-workflows.mjs` and `executor-workflow-secrets.mjs`, "the converge writes/stamps" means that module's workflow-writing step, so I left it.
- **Two recorded changes lack a provenance entry:** `basics/pack.mjs` (`_pack.md`) and `improve-comments/checks.mjs` (`improve-comments-scope.md`). Both provenance files are empty, and the tool only accepts a `born` entry first, so these wait for the backfill. `check_the_work` flags them as advisory.
- **Long-dash advisories:** these are on lines I edited or files I renamed; the dashes were already there. I kept the declared-check wording "the update … skips the home" without re-checking that the update actually skips the canon repo.

**Diff reach:** the change touched about 130 files across engine, docs, tests and ten packs. That's the size of a vocabulary sweep rather than a design problem; generated text and `@real-entity` test comments add a lot of it.

-# Fleet baseline — force every member to baseline now

-**This task runs no agent, and no schedule.** It declares `trigger: request`, with `agent_model: none`: the scheduler run never asks it, and the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) → [`force-fleet-baseline.mjs`](force-fleet-baseline.mjs) the executor runs as code-work when — and only when — a human creates an item for it. This file is the human-facing record of what that is; there is no agent phase.
-Create the work item, from a checkout of this repo with `GITHUB_TOKEN` set:
-REPOS=Alpha Beta            ← limit to these repos (bare name or owner/name, SPACE-separated); omit for every covered member
-DRY_RUN=true                ← report what would fire, fire nothing
-INCLUDE_DORMANT=true        ← dormant members are skipped by default — they stopped their own scheduler on purpose
-FOLLOW_MINUTES=30           ← how long to follow members to current before giving up on what is left (default 20)

-Values are space-separated because the parameter bag splits `KEY=value` pairs on commas. The two safety knobs are read from the item's Context and from nowhere else: an item created without them runs unscoped and live.

-Enumerate every repo under the configured owner over the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` PAT and, for each **covered, non-dormant** member, dispatch that member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` with `wake: update` — the same button the owner would press in that repo's Actions tab, pressed across the fleet in one run. The wake lever names one task, so each member does exactly one thing: converge its mount.

-Nothing is baselined *here*, and nothing is written to any member — no commit, no issue, no comment. Each member converges its own mount, with its own token, under its own scheduler and delivery policy; if its converge needs an agent, that member's own executor runs it. The enforcer **dispatches**; the member **executes**. That is the whole trust model: no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access, and the one fleet credential is the PAT with Actions write.

-Then it **follows** each dispatched member until that member's own `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps the engine and every declared pack at the versions canon publishes — reusing the comparison [`fleet-roster`](../fleet-roster/) already makes for its drift issues.
-Every repo under the owner lands in the run summary under exactly one state — so a fleet-wide force is never mistaken for fleet-wide coverage. Dispatched members are reported by **outcome**:
-converged           ← was behind canon, and reached its versions during this run
-already-current     ← was at canon's versions before the dispatch, so its own update correctly declined
-did-not-converge    ← its scheduler ran and it is still behind — go and read that run
-never-started       ← the dispatch was accepted and no run followed it
-unknown             ← the member could not be read
-`already-current` is a **success**. A member at canon's versions has nothing to do, its `update` precondition says so, and demanding work of it would report a fault where there is none.

-Freshness here is the **published version numbers**. Canon content that shipped without a version bump moves no number, so a member can read `already-current` while lacking canon's newest commit ([#1292](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1292)). The report says this itself rather than letting the word imply more than was checked.

-The old follow was a blind fixed wait: every run paid it in full, whatever the fleet was doing, which is what forced the lever to be a standalone workflow. The typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs the old workflow offered are carried by the item's Context above.

import re,subprocess
files=subprocess.check_output(['git','diff','--name-only','--diff-filter=U'],text=True).split()
pat=re.compile(r'<<<<<<< HEAD\n(.*?)=======\n(.*?)>>>>>>> [^\n]*\n', re.S)
for p in files:
    s=open(p).read()
    if p.endswith('pack.mjs'):
        s=pat.sub(lambda m: m.group(2).replace("minEngineVersion: '60822.1'","minEngineVersion: '60925.1'"), s)
    else:
        def f(m):
            ours,theirs=m.group(1),m.group(2)
            i=ours.find('## 2026-09-25')
            assert i>=0,p
            mine=ours[i:]
            # skip entries main already has
            entries=re.split(r'(?=^## )',mine,flags=re.M)
            add=''.join(e for e in entries if e.strip() and e.split('\n')[0] not in theirs)
            return theirs.rstrip('\n')+'\n\n'+add
        s=pat.sub(f,s)
    assert '<<<<<<<' not in s
    open(p,'w').write(s)
    print('ok',p)
EOF

-- **Mechanism:** the sweep keeps calling the dormancy predicate the `claudinite-tasks` pack now

-## 2026-09-25 · reworded · renamed from fleet-baseline, its file moved with it
-- **Reason:** owner decision retiring the baseline vocabulary: the lever forces each member's
-  update, so it is named for it. The report's `converged`/`did-not-converge` outcomes became
-- **Rejected:** renaming the sweep's `FLEET_BASELINE_*` environment knobs: a hand-run still setting
-  the old `DRY_RUN` name would run live.
-# Fleet update — force every member to update now

-**This task runs no agent, and no schedule.** It declares `trigger: request`, with `agent_model: none`: the scheduler run never asks it, and the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) → [`force-fleet-update.mjs`](force-fleet-update.mjs) the executor runs as code-work when — and only when — a human creates an item for it. This file is the human-facing record of what that is; there is no agent phase.
-Create the work item, from a checkout of this repo with `GITHUB_TOKEN` set:
-REPOS=Alpha Beta            ← limit to these repos (bare name or owner/name, SPACE-separated); omit for every covered member
-DRY_RUN=true                ← report what would fire, fire nothing
-INCLUDE_DORMANT=true        ← dormant members are skipped by default — they stopped their own scheduler on purpose
-FOLLOW_MINUTES=30           ← how long to follow members to current before giving up on what is left (default 20)

-Values are space-separated because the parameter bag splits `KEY=value` pairs on commas. The two safety knobs are read from the item's Context and from nowhere else: an item created without them runs unscoped and live.

-Enumerate every repo under the configured owner over the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` PAT and, for each **covered, non-dormant** member, dispatch that member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` with `wake: update` — the same button the owner would press in that repo's Actions tab, pressed across the fleet in one run. The wake lever names one task, so each member does exactly one thing: update its mount.

-Nothing is updated *here*, and nothing is written to any member — no commit, no issue, no comment. Each member updates its own mount, with its own token, under its own scheduler and delivery policy; if its update needs an agent, that member's own executor runs it. The enforcer **dispatches**; the member **executes**. That is the whole trust model: no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access, and the one fleet credential is the PAT with Actions write.

-Then it **follows** each dispatched member until that member's own `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps the engine and every declared pack at the versions canon publishes — reusing the comparison [`fleet-roster`](../fleet-roster/) already makes for its drift issues.
-Every repo under the owner lands in the run summary under exactly one state — so a fleet-wide force is never mistaken for fleet-wide coverage. Dispatched members are reported by **outcome**:
-updated             ← was behind canon, and reached its versions during this run
-already-current     ← was at canon's versions before the dispatch, so its own update correctly declined
-did-not-update      ← its scheduler ran and it is still behind — go and read that run
-never-started       ← the dispatch was accepted and no run followed it
-unknown             ← the member could not be read
-`already-current` is a **success**. A member at canon's versions has nothing to do, its `update` precondition says so, and demanding work of it would report a fault where there is none.

-Freshness here is the **published version numbers**. Canon content that shipped without a version bump moves no number, so a member can read `already-current` while lacking canon's newest commit ([#1292](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1292)). The report says this itself rather than letting the word imply more than was checked.
-## Why this is not the retired 45-minute sleep

-The old follow was a blind fixed wait: every run paid it in full, whatever the fleet was doing, which is what forced the lever to be a standalone workflow. [`follow-to-current.mjs`](follow-to-current.mjs) polls a **real terminal condition** instead — each member leaves the loop the moment it reads current. An already-current fleet finishes on the first pass, in seconds. Only a member genuinely mid-update costs any waiting, and the budget (`FOLLOW_MINUTES`) bounds even that.
-## Why a task and not a workflow (any more)

-The standalone `fleet-baseline.yml` workflow (retired 2026-08-11, #749) lived in the enforcer's `.github/` — the one place the nightly update can never push (#649), so every change to it crossed the fleet by the slow withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path. As a task, the lever ships with the ordinary vendor refresh like everything else, and the repo's vendored scheduler stays its **only** workflow. The typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs the old workflow offered are carried by the item's Context above.

-A member that could not be dispatched — a missing scheduler workflow, a PAT without Actions write, a workflow GitHub disabled — is named in the summary and the sweep exits non-zero. **So is a member that was dispatched and never reached canon's versions**: that is the failure this whole follow exists to surface, and the one the dispatch-count report used to show as a success. The executor parks the item, so either escalates rather than silently leaving part of the fleet behind.
-## Why the declaration reads as it does
-Carried over from the declaration's comments when it became `task.json`.
-claudinite-fleet-sheepdog task: fleet-update — the enforcer's MANUAL lever: force every covered
-member (or the ones named) to update NOW instead of at its next occurrence.
-`trigger: request` — the first task off the schedule (#749). It answers no recurring
-question, so nothing asks it; the ONLY way it runs is a work item created by hand,
-optionally carrying its parameters as Context lines:
-  --context "REPOS=Alpha Beta"        (optional — omit for every covered member; space-separated)
-  --context "DRY_RUN=true"            (optional — report what would fire, fire nothing)
-  --context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"    (optional — dormant members are skipped by default)
-  --context "FOLLOW_MINUTES=30"       (optional — how long to follow members to current)
-This replaces the pack's standalone fleet-baseline WORKFLOW (retired 2026-08-11,
-#749). The workflow existed for two reasons that are both gone: its FOLLOW half
-(watch every member to a terminal state — a 45-minute sleep no serialized run
-should hold) is given up, and its typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs are carried by
-the item's Context instead. What the workflow shape COST is what this shape
-recovers: the `.github/` managed copy was the one file the nightly update could
-not push (#649's withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path), while a task rides the
-`agent_model: 'none'` — pure code. The whole pass is the dispatch sweep
-(force-fleet-update.mjs, invoked by worker.mjs): enumerate the fleet over the
-PAT, wake each covered member's own `update` item, follow each one until it stamps
-canon's published versions, and report the full roster by OUTCOME (#1293). Nothing
-agentic happens HERE — each member's own update may hand off to that member's own
-agent, which is the fan-out model's point: the enforcer dispatches, the member
-executes, and no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access.
-Never due on its own — `manual` means the scheduler run never instantiates
-this task, so an item exists ONLY because a human created one, and that IS the
-The dispatch half is one enumeration plus a declaration read and one POST per
-member — under a minute. What sizes this bound is the FOLLOW (#1293): the sweep
-stays until every dispatched member stamps canon's versions, and a member's own
-update takes 5–10 minutes end to end. The follow gives up at
-DEFAULT_FOLLOW_MINUTES (20) and reports what it was still waiting on, so this
-must sit above that with room for the dispatch walk and the final probe —
-otherwise the platform kills the run at the bound and the report is never
-printed, which is the one outcome worse than a slow one.

import re,subprocess
files=subprocess.check_output(['git','diff','--name-only','--diff-filter=U'],text=True).split()
pat=re.compile(r'<<<<<<< [^\n]*\n(.*?)(?:\|\|\|\|\|\|\| [^\n]*\n.*?)?=======\n(.*?)>>>>>>> [^\n]*\n', re.S)
for p in files:
    s=open(p).read()
    def f(m):
        a,b=m.group(1),m.group(2)
        # a = upstream (main) side during rebase, b = our commit side
        entries=re.split(r'(?=^## )',b,flags=re.M)
        add=''.join(e for e in entries if e.startswith('## 2026-09-25') and e.split('\n')[0] not in a)
        add=re.sub(r'- \*\*Model:\*\* [^\n]*\n','',add)
        return a.rstrip('\n')+'\n\n'+add if add else a
    s=pat.sub(f,s)
    s=re.sub(r'\n{3,}','\n\n',s)
    assert '<<<<<<<' not in s, p
    open(p,'w').write(s); print('ok',p)
EOF

-## 2026-08-11 · born · the operator's lever to force every member to baseline now (#750)

-- **Reason:** the fan-out model is what works: the enforcer presses each member's own scheduler
-  button and everything agentic happens inside the member. Under per-project scheduling the fleet
-  needs no push in the ordinary case; this is for the un-ordinary ones.
-- **Mechanism:** an agentless task on the ordinary work-item queue rather than a workflow, never due

-  `.github/` managed copy that only the withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path could deliver.
-## 2026-08-23 · reworded · the lever reports outcomes, not dispatches (#1294)
-- **Reason:** a dispatch returning 204 says a run was queued and nothing more. A report built from
-  those 204s describes the sweep's own outgoing calls while reading as fleet-wide delivery: one run
-  announced 13 fired, 0 failed where 9 of the 13 took nothing. The sweep now follows each member to
-  a terminal condition read off the member itself and fails the run when a dispatched member never
-  got there. `already-current` is kept a success of its own, because folding it into a failure
-  reports a fault that is not there and into `converged` claims work that did not happen.

-  bag (the task's declared secrets and the Action token among it) and renders the verdict it returns

-- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner), who asked why every task re-implements one runner's job.
-# Fleet baseline — force every member to baseline now

-**This task runs no agent, and no schedule.** It declares `trigger: request`, with `agent_model: none`: the scheduler run never asks it, and the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) → [`force-fleet-baseline.mjs`](force-fleet-baseline.mjs) the executor runs as code-work when — and only when — a human creates an item for it. This file is the human-facing record of what that is; there is no agent phase.
-Create the work item, from a checkout of this repo with `GITHUB_TOKEN` set:
-REPOS=Alpha Beta            ← limit to these repos (bare name or owner/name, SPACE-separated); omit for every covered member
-DRY_RUN=true                ← report what would fire, fire nothing
-INCLUDE_DORMANT=true        ← dormant members are skipped by default — they stopped their own scheduler on purpose
-FOLLOW_MINUTES=30           ← how long to follow members to current before giving up on what is left (default 20)

-Values are space-separated because the parameter bag splits `KEY=value` pairs on commas. The two safety knobs are read from the item's Context and from nowhere else: an item created without them runs unscoped and live.

-Enumerate every repo under the configured owner over the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` PAT and, for each **covered, non-dormant** member, dispatch that member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` with `wake: update` — the same button the owner would press in that repo's Actions tab, pressed across the fleet in one run. The wake lever names one task, so each member does exactly one thing: converge its mount.

-Nothing is baselined *here*, and nothing is written to any member — no commit, no issue, no comment. Each member converges its own mount, with its own token, under its own scheduler and delivery policy; if its converge needs an agent, that member's own executor runs it. The enforcer **dispatches**; the member **executes**. That is the whole trust model: no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access, and the one fleet credential is the PAT with Actions write.

-Then it **follows** each dispatched member until that member's own `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps the engine and every declared pack at the versions canon publishes — reusing the comparison [`fleet-roster`](../fleet-roster/) already makes for its drift issues.
-Every repo under the owner lands in the run summary under exactly one state — so a fleet-wide force is never mistaken for fleet-wide coverage. Dispatched members are reported by **outcome**:
-converged           ← was behind canon, and reached its versions during this run
-already-current     ← was at canon's versions before the dispatch, so its own update correctly declined
-did-not-converge    ← its scheduler ran and it is still behind — go and read that run
-never-started       ← the dispatch was accepted and no run followed it
-unknown             ← the member could not be read
-`already-current` is a **success**. A member at canon's versions has nothing to do, its `update` precondition says so, and demanding work of it would report a fault where there is none.

-Freshness here is the **published version numbers**. Canon content that shipped without a version bump moves no number, so a member can read `already-current` while lacking canon's newest commit ([#1292](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1292)). The report says this itself rather than letting the word imply more than was checked.
-## Why this is not the retired 45-minute sleep

-The old follow was a blind fixed wait: every run paid it in full, whatever the fleet was doing, which is what forced the lever to be a standalone workflow. [`follow-to-current.mjs`](follow-to-current.mjs) polls a **real terminal condition** instead — each member leaves the loop the moment it reads current. An already-current fleet finishes on the first pass, in seconds. Only a member genuinely mid-converge costs any waiting, and the budget (`FOLLOW_MINUTES`) bounds even that.
-## Why a task and not a workflow (any more)

-The standalone `fleet-baseline.yml` workflow (retired 2026-08-11, #749) lived in the enforcer's `.github/` — the one place the nightly converge can never push (#649), so every change to it crossed the fleet by the slow withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path. As a task, the lever ships with the ordinary vendor refresh like everything else, and the repo's vendored scheduler stays its **only** workflow. The typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs the old workflow offered are carried by the item's Context above.

-A member that could not be dispatched — a missing scheduler workflow, a PAT without Actions write, a workflow GitHub disabled — is named in the summary and the sweep exits non-zero. **So is a member that was dispatched and never reached canon's versions**: that is the failure this whole follow exists to surface, and the one the dispatch-count report used to show as a success. The executor parks the item, so either escalates rather than silently leaving part of the fleet behind.
-## Why the declaration reads as it does
-Carried over from the declaration's comments when it became `task.json`.
-claudinite-fleet-sheepdog task: fleet-baseline — the enforcer's MANUAL lever: force every covered
-member (or the ones named) to baseline NOW instead of at its next occurrence.
-`trigger: request` — the first task off the schedule (#749). It answers no recurring
-question, so nothing asks it; the ONLY way it runs is a work item created by hand,
-optionally carrying its parameters as Context lines:
-  --context "REPOS=Alpha Beta"        (optional — omit for every covered member; space-separated)
-  --context "DRY_RUN=true"            (optional — report what would fire, fire nothing)
-  --context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"    (optional — dormant members are skipped by default)
-  --context "FOLLOW_MINUTES=30"       (optional — how long to follow members to current)
-This replaces the pack's standalone fleet-baseline WORKFLOW (retired 2026-08-11,
-#749). The workflow existed for two reasons that are both gone: its FOLLOW half
-(watch every member to a terminal state — a 45-minute sleep no serialized run
-should hold) is given up, and its typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs are carried by
-the item's Context instead. What the workflow shape COST is what this shape
-recovers: the `.github/` managed copy was the one file the nightly converge could
-not push (#649's withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path), while a task rides the
-`agent_model: 'none'` — pure code. The whole pass is the dispatch sweep
-(force-fleet-baseline.mjs, invoked by worker.mjs): enumerate the fleet over the
-PAT, wake each covered member's own `update` item, follow each one until it stamps
-canon's published versions, and report the full roster by OUTCOME (#1293). Nothing
-agentic happens HERE — each member's own converge may hand off to that member's own
-agent, which is the fan-out model's point: the enforcer dispatches, the member
-executes, and no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access.
-Never due on its own — `manual` means the scheduler run never instantiates
-this task, so an item exists ONLY because a human created one, and that IS the
-The dispatch half is one enumeration plus a declaration read and one POST per
-member — under a minute. What sizes this bound is the FOLLOW (#1293): the sweep
-stays until every dispatched member stamps canon's versions, and a member's own
-update takes 5–10 minutes end to end. The follow gives up at
-DEFAULT_FOLLOW_MINUTES (20) and reports what it was still waiting on, so this
-must sit above that with room for the dispatch walk and the final probe —
-otherwise the platform kills the run at the bound and the report is never
-printed, which is the one outcome worse than a slow one.

- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to re-vendor a repo's mount to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes - the entry on its provenance file, which kind, and how to append it - and what a pack's README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, skills, checks, tasks, manifest, README or provenance folder, in a repo's local pack or on a canon's shelf.
- extract-packs-from-a-project: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the basics task lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve a repo's own comments as a pass of their own: delete, correct, add the why. Use when working a repo's comments deliberately (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production. Use when designing a larger element, when filing a migration plan's chain, when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: How a plan's phases are ordered so nothing stalls mid-run. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan (including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file), when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.

Owner terminology decisions of 2026-09-25 (research: `product-wiki/Terminology/divergences/README.md` in missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite).

## 1. `severity: blocking | advisory` → `on_fail: block | advise`

- **The rename:** every declared check (121 entries), every coded check, the engine's findings pipeline (`finding`, `applyGrace`, `applyConfig`, the report, the PreToolUse judge) and the settings overrides (`"off" | "advise" | "block"`) now use `on_fail`.
- **Unchanged, by owner decision:**
  - report text still prints `[BLOCKING]` / `[ADVISORY]` and `N blocking, M advisory`;
  - the pack READMEs' Severity (impact) and Enforcement columns;
  - the usage counters, which the usage fold parses from that report text;
  - the provenance kind `severity-changed`.
- **Legacy tolerance, one week (owner):**
  - The engine still reads `severity` on a rule, a declaration, a finding and an override.
  - It also mirrors `severity` on every finding, so a member's own tests that read `finding.severity` stay green.
  - The removal is [#2319](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2319): blocked by this PR, not before 2026-10-02, `Automerge: anything`, with its full patch written and tested.
- **Advisory:** `legacy-shape-in-use` now names two kinds of leftover:
  - an override still spelled `blocking` / `advisory`;
  - a local pack's declared or coded check that still carries `severity`.
- **Migration record** `engine/migrations/2026-09-25-on-fail-rename` (codemod `renameOnFail`):
  - respells the member's own settings overrides, local declared checks and local check modules in one update pass;
  - applies only once the member's mount holds the engine that reads `on_fail`;
  - leaves the member's tests and the vendored mount alone.
- **Release:**
  - The engine is released as `60925.1`; the canary rehearsal ([run 36165536547](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/36165536547)) passed against `ae7834ab`.
  - Every pack's `minEngineVersion` rises to it, because an older engine throws on a declared check with no `severity`.
  - No forced fleet push (owner): the nightly update carries it.
- **Side fix:** `named-import-of-new-engine-export` read an edited export line (a changed signature, an `ENGINE_VERSION` bump) as a brand-new export. The added-lines value source now drops a value that a removed line of the same file also carried.

## 2. Retire the baseline / converge vocabulary

- **`adopt-claudinite` description:** says "re-vendor a repo's mount to pick up updates" instead of "baseline a repo".
- **`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`'s `fleet-baseline` task becomes `fleet-update`:** task id, worker, `force-fleet-update.mjs` and tests move. The pack record `2026-09-25-fleet-update-rename` rewrites the old id in members' `taskScheduler.disabledTasks`, the only place a member holds it.
- **Live prose:** "the baseline pack" reads basics; "baseline migration" reads migration record; "converge" in the nightly-update sense reads "update".
- **Left alone on purpose:**
  - "converge" for a work item reaching its end state (`converge-item.mjs`);
  - module names (`converge-wiring.mjs`);
  - the test sense of "baseline" and research-project's "naive baseline";
  - history: design docs, existing migration records, provenance.
- **Also changed:** both generated index headers now say "every update", so every member's two index files are rewritten once on their next update.

## Reach

This change touches most packs, because every check's declaration carries the renamed field; most of the 627 files are one-line `on_fail` edits and their provenance entries. A field read by every check can't be renamed in one place. The 133 `no-new-long-dashes` advisories are dashes already on lines the vocabulary sweep reworded.

Both renames are done and green in one PR, [missingbulb/claudinite#2318](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2318), ready for your review. The suite passes (3991/3991) and the world and work sweeps have nothing blocking.

**Where the brief was off:**
- There are 121 declared checks, not 98.
- Members' own local packs also carry `severity`, not only their settings. A new migration record rewrites the old spelling in their settings, local declared checks and local check modules in one update pass. `legacy-shape-in-use` flags whatever that pass misses.
- Members' own tests that read `finding.severity` would have broken on the engine update. The engine therefore also sets `severity` on every finding until the old spelling comes out.
- An older engine throws on a declared check without `severity`. So the engine is released as `60925.1` and every pack now requires it. The canary rehearsal ran against this branch and passed ([run 36165536547](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/36165536547)); the release notes (`engine/RELEASES.md`) carry the row.

**What I did on your answers:**
- The report text (`[BLOCKING]`, `2 blocking, 1 advisory`), the READMEs' Enforcement column and the usage counters keep "blocking"/"advisory".
- The removal is filed as [#2319](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2319): blocked until this PR merges, not before 2026-10-02, auto-merge when green. Its full patch is in the issue body and its tests pass on this branch.
- No forced fleet push; the nightly update carries it.

**Beyond the brief:** the `named-import-of-new-engine-export` check read any edited export line as a new export, so every engine version bump tripped it. I fixed that in the engine, since this change needed it.

**Part 2** (done by a background agent, then brought onto this branch):
- The `adopt-claudinite` description no longer says "baseline".
- The fleet sheepdog's `fleet-baseline` task is now `fleet-update`, with a migration record for the one place members hold its id.
- "The baseline pack", "baseline migration" and "converge" meaning the nightly update now read basics, migration record and update.

**Left as they are; you may want to look at these:**
- The fleet-update sweep's `FLEET_BASELINE_*` environment variables kept their names. A hand-run using an old name like `DRY_RUN` after a later rename would run live instead of dry.
- A local rule still says "`basics/baselining` is the deliberate exception", and that task no longer exists.
- The agent suspects `provenance-marking`'s far-ahead record version makes a fresh install of `claudinite-growth` skip some pack versions. I haven't checked it.
- The provenance kind `severity-changed` keeps its name, since existing entries use it.
- 133 long-dash advisories remain. They are on lines the vocabulary sweep reworded, where the dashes already were.

Folders the change touched (not counting tests, READMEs and provenance):
```
engine/                    engine 60925.1; on_fail pipeline; old-spelling reads; the new migration record
packs/*/ (every pack)      declared and coded checks use on_fail; minEngineVersion 60925.1
packs/claudinite-lifecycle legacy-shape-in-use flags the old spelling; adopt-claudinite trigger text
packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog  fleet-baseline → fleet-update, plus its rename record
packs/basics, -growth, -canon-curation  prose reworded: on_fail; baseline/converge → basics/update
.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite  consumer-safe-change reads both spellings; rules reworded
vendoring/rehearsal        fixture on_fail
```

# Working with generated files

- **Working with a file a test or tool generates** — put `GENERATED` in its name, and don't
  hand-edit it; change the generator. Never resolve its merge conflict by hand: clear the
  markers with either side, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit that
  output. Consider automating the clear with a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry, and
  `git rerere` for a conflict that recurs. (working-file-test)

- **A generator whose OWN set of outputs grows on its own** — one baseline per auto-discovered
  category (a new test "kind", a new fixture), rather than a fixed, named list — needs its
  `merge=ours` coverage to auto-track that growth too, typically a glob or pattern in
  `.gitattributes` rather than one entry per file. A per-file allowlist silently stops covering
  the moment a new category starts committing its own baselines, and the gap surfaces as a
  binary merge conflict git cannot 3-way-merge at all — at the worst possible moment, mid-merge,
  for a category nobody remembered to wire up. (generator-whose-own)

# Writing Claudinite skills

A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all — and `body: workflow` or `body: guidelines` under `metadata` too, saying which kind of body follows; the growth pack's `writing-pack-prose` says how to choose) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). A skill may own the rules that validate its action — `checks.mjs` beside the SKILL.md, one module per rule, with their fixture tests under the owning pack's `test/` mirroring the skill's path; shape and the relevance-first gate in [engine/checks/README.md](../../../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule). Ownership is placement: the skill lives in exactly one owning pack's `skills/` — there is no skill catalog; the pack's own README names what it bundles. Instruction-writing *quality* — how agents actually follow docs — is [authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md)' turf; this skill is the corpus mechanics. (1)
